newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy wants EU "flexibility" in defence, justice.
newsitem.headline: Italy wants EU "flexibility" in defence, justice.

text.p: Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said in an interview published on Sunday that Italy wanted the EU's new treaty to provide for possible faster integration between some member states in defence, justice and public order.

Dini told Corriere della Sera newspaper that Italy believed flexibility -- the European Union buzzword for the concept of allowing some countries to forge ahead faster than others -- should not be applicable in some areas, such as foreign policy.
"The use of flexibility should be encouraged on the other hand in sectors such as security and defence, justice and public order," he said in an interview from Brussels.
But he said the use of majority voting was more appropriate than flexibility in the foreign policy of the 15-nation bloc.
"To be credible, the EU's foreign policy must be unified and cannot be compromised by sectoral initiatives," Dini said.
"The paralysis and slowness that we have seen in the past must be overcome not with flexibility but with a large recourse to decisions taken by majority."
France and Germany are pushing for a flexibility clause to be introduced into the EU treaty, currently under review in the inter-governmental conference (IGC) due to be completed in June.

Under a proposal put forward last year by Paris and Bonn, a broad clause on flexibility would be written into the treaty, but no single country would be allowed a veto to block others who wanted to pool national sovereignty.
Britain, Sweden, Denmark and Portugal are wary of moves to do away with unanimity and fear the creation of an inner core of countries that could set the rules without the others.

Dini said that certain core EU tenets, such as European citizenship, free movement of goods, people and services, agriculture and fishing policy, competition and trade policy and development were inappropriate for "enhanced cooperation", as the concept of flexibility is sometimes known.
He said flexibility should be approved case by case but there should also be a way of ensuring that states who did not immediately join in certain initiatives could do so later.
Dini said that Italy would prefer, in general, for all countries to move forward together but that Rome was ready to participate in enhanced cooperation initiatives.
